levels.title: Probability & Statistics: The Big Picture
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the two big jobs of this tree: describing many cases with a few numbers, and measuring how likely things are.

levels.title: What a Percent Really Is
levels.objective: After this level you can turn "3 out of 20" into a percentage and explain that percent simply means "out of every 100".

levels.title: Percent Change
levels.objective: After this level you can work out how much something rose or fell in percent by comparing the change with where it started.

levels.title: Up 50%, Down 50%
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a 50% drop followed by a 50% rise leaves you worse off than where you began.

levels.title: Percent vs. Percentage Points
levels.objective: After this level you can tell a rise of 5 percentage points from a rise of 5 percent, and spot a headline that mixes them up.

levels.title: Rates: Counting Per Person
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why comparing totals between a big place and a small one misleads, and why rates per person fix it.

levels.title: "1 in 3" Beats 33%
levels.objective: After this level you can switch between percentages, fractions and "1 in N" counts, and explain why counts of people are easier to picture.

levels.title: How Big Is a Billion?
levels.objective: After this level you can picture the difference between a thousand, a million and a billion using seconds of time.

levels.title: Too Precise to Be True
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a number can look more exact than the measurement behind it, using the 98.6 degree fever line.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Making Sense of Numbers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what percentages, percentage points, rates and big numbers really say, and spot when one is misused.

levels.title: The Mean: Add Up and Share Out
levels.objective: After this level you can find the mean of a set of numbers and explain it as the amount each would get if the total were shared equally.

levels.title: The Median: The Middle One
levels.objective: After this level you can find the median by lining values up in order and explain why it is the "typical" middle case.

levels.title: When Mean and Median Disagree
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a few very large values pull the mean far above the median, as with incomes and house prices.

levels.title: The Mode: Most Popular Wins
levels.objective: After this level you can find the mode and explain when the most common value is the most useful average, as with shoe sizes.

levels.title: Outliers
levels.objective: After this level you can spot an outlier and decide whether it is a mistake to fix or a real case worth keeping.

levels.title: Same Average, Different Spread
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why two sets with the same average can be very different, and measure the gap with the range.

levels.title: Spread in One Number
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the standard deviation in plain words as the typical distance of values from the average.

levels.title: The Bell Curve
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the bell curve, where most values bunch near the middle, and name everyday measurements that follow it.

levels.title: Percentiles
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what being in the 90th percentile means, using children's growth charts and test scores.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Averages and Spread
levels.objective: After this level you can choose the right average for a set of numbers and describe how spread out it is.

levels.title: What a Probability Is
levels.objective: After this level you can place a chance on the scale from impossible (0) to certain (1) and explain it as a long-run share of outcomes.

levels.title: Counting the Outcomes
levels.objective: After this level you can list the equally likely outcomes of two dice and explain why 7 is the most common total.

levels.title: Chances That Multiply
levels.objective: After this level you can work out the chance of two independent things both happening, like rolling two sixes, by multiplying.

levels.title: The Chance of At Least One
levels.objective: After this level you can work out the chance of "at least one" by first finding the chance of none, as with a six in four rolls.

levels.title: Coins Have No Memory
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what makes events independent and why a coin that landed heads five times is still 50/50.

levels.title: The Gambler's Fallacy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the gambler's fallacy using the 1913 Monte Carlo roulette run where black came up 26 times.

levels.title: Streaks and Clumps
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why truly random sequences contain more streaks and clusters than people expect.

levels.title: The Law of Large Numbers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why results settle close to the true chance over many tries but swing wildly over a few.

levels.title: The Birthday Problem
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why 23 people are enough for a better than even chance that two share a birthday.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How Chance Works
levels.objective: After this level you can work out simple chances with dice and coins, and explain why luck does not "even out" in the short run.

levels.title: Odds and Probability
levels.objective: After this level you can turn odds like "3 to 1 against" into a probability and back again.

levels.title: Expected Value
levels.objective: After this level you can work out the average result of a bet over many plays by weighing each outcome by its chance.

levels.title: Why the Casino Always Wins
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the house edge, using the extra green pockets on an American roulette wheel.

levels.title: The Math of the Lottery
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the odds of winning a big jackpot with everyday chances and explain why a ticket's expected value is below its price.

levels.title: Is Insurance a Bad Bet?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why insurance loses money on average for buyers yet can still be a sensible choice.

levels.title: The Monty Hall Puzzle
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why switching doors in the Monty Hall puzzle wins two times out of three.

levels.title: Should You Risk the Parking Ticket?
levels.objective: After this level you can use expected value to compare two everyday choices, like paying for parking or risking a fine.

levels.title: Same Average, Different Risk
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why two choices with the same expected value can differ in how badly things might go.

levels.title: Let the Computer Roll the Dice
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how running thousands of pretend trials on a computer estimates a chance too hard to calculate.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Bets and Expected Value
levels.objective: After this level you can judge a bet or an everyday gamble by its odds and its expected value.

levels.title: Absolute Risk: The Real Numbers
levels.objective: After this level you can state a risk as an absolute number, like 2 in 1,000, and explain why that is the number that matters to you.

levels.title: Relative Risk: "Doubles Your Risk!"
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why "doubles your risk" can mean going from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000, and ask for the absolute numbers.

levels.title: How Many Must Take the Pill?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the number needed to treat: how many people take a treatment for one of them to benefit.

levels.title: Is Flying Safer Than Driving?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a risk comparison depends on what you count per: per trip, per mile or per hour.

levels.title: Base Rates: Start With How Common
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why you should start with how common something is before judging a single case.

levels.title: Two Ways a Test Can Be Right
levels.objective: After this level you can explain a test's sensitivity (catching true cases) and specificity (clearing healthy people) in plain words.

levels.title: Why Most Positives Can Be False
levels.objective: After this level you can show with a count of 10,000 people why a good test for a rare condition can give mostly false alarms.

levels.title: Changing Your Mind by the Right Amount
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Bayes' idea in words: start from the base rate and let each new piece of evidence shift it.

levels.title: The Prosecutor's Fallacy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a tiny chance of the evidence happening by accident is not the chance of innocence, using the Sally Clark case.

levels.title: Milestone: Thinking in Chances
levels.objective: After this level you can connect percentages, averages, chance, expected value and base rates to judge one real-world risk.

levels.title: Tasting the Soup: Why We Sample
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a small sample can describe a whole population, the way one spoonful tells you about a pot of soup.

levels.title: Random Means Everyone Gets a Chance
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a fair sample gives every member of the population the same chance of being picked.

levels.title: The Poll That Picked the Wrong Winner
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the 1936 Literary Digest poll got 2 million answers and still called the election wrong.

levels.title: Why 1,000 People Are Enough
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a random sample of about 1,000 can describe a whole country, whatever its size.

levels.title: What "Plus or Minus 3" Means
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a poll's margin of error covers and why a lead smaller than it is too close to call.

levels.title: The People Who Don't Answer
levels.objective: After this level you can explain nonresponse bias: why the people who skip a survey can skew its results.

levels.title: Weighting: Fixing a Lopsided Sample
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how pollsters weight answers so a sample's mix of ages and backgrounds matches the population.

levels.title: The Wording Changes the Answer
levels.objective: After this level you can spot how the wording and order of survey questions can shift the answers people give.

levels.title: Click Polls and Online Reviews
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why polls where people choose to take part measure who cares most, not what most people think.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Samples and Polls
levels.objective: After this level you can judge whether a poll or survey can be trusted from how its sample was drawn and its questions asked.

levels.title: Watching vs. Testing
levels.objective: After this level you can tell an observational study, which watches what people already do, from an experiment, which changes something.

levels.title: The Control Group
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why an experiment needs a comparison group, using James Lind's 1747 scurvy trial.

levels.title: Why Flip a Coin to Pick Groups
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how random assignment balances hidden differences between groups, which is why it makes a fair test.

levels.title: Placebos and Blinding
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why trials use placebos and keep people blind to who got what.

levels.title: Comparing Like With Like
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a hidden third factor can distort a comparison and how studies adjust for it by comparing similar groups.

levels.title: How Strong Is a Link?
levels.objective: After this level you can read a scatter plot and explain what a correlation near 0, near 1 or below 0 says about how closely two things move together.

levels.title: What "Statistically Significant" Means
levels.objective: After this level you can explain honestly what a significant result and a p-value tell you: how surprising the data would be if nothing were going on.

levels.title: Significant Isn't the Same as Big
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a result can be statistically significant yet too small to matter, and why effect size counts.

levels.title: Do It Again: Replication
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why one study is rarely enough and what happened when scientists tried to repeat published results.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Experiments and Evidence
levels.objective: After this level you can judge how strong a study's evidence is from its design: control group, randomization, blinding and size.

levels.title: Reading Any Chart
levels.objective: After this level you can read a chart by checking its title, axes, units and source before looking at its shape.

levels.title: The Chopped-Off Axis
levels.objective: After this level you can spot a bar chart whose axis doesn't start at zero and explain how it makes small gaps look huge.

levels.title: Picking the Start Date
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how choosing where a chart starts and ends can make the same trend look like a rise or a fall.

levels.title: Maps That Show Where People Live
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why many maps of totals simply show where people live, and why per person maps tell more.

levels.title: Pies, Pictures and 3D Tricks
levels.objective: After this level you can spot pie charts that don't add to 100% and pictures that exaggerate by growing in two directions at once.

levels.title: Two Axes, One Story
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a chart with two different vertical scales can make any two lines seem to move together.

levels.title: Log Scales
levels.objective: After this level you can read a chart where each step up the axis multiplies instead of adds, and explain when that helps.

levels.title: Running Totals Always Go Up
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a cumulative chart keeps climbing even when things are slowing down.

levels.title: Error Bars and Storm Cones
levels.objective: After this level you can read error bars and a hurricane forecast cone as ranges of uncertainty, not as sizes.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Graphs That Mislead
levels.objective: After this level you can take apart a misleading chart and redraw its story fairly in words.

levels.title: Simpson's Paradox
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a trend in every group can reverse when the groups are combined, using the 1973 Berkeley admissions data.

levels.title: Regression to the Mean
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why an extreme result is usually followed by a more ordinary one, with no cause needed.

levels.title: Why Remedies Seem to Work
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how regression to the mean makes a treatment or a new rule look effective when people start at their worst.

levels.title: Small Places, Extreme Numbers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the smallest groups show both the highest and the lowest rates, just by chance.

levels.title: How Filters Create Fake Links
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how studying only a selected group can create a link between two traits that isn't there in everyone.

levels.title: Test Enough Things, Something Wins
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why testing many ideas at once guarantees some "significant" flukes, and how p-hacking exploits that.

levels.title: Cancer Clusters and Random Clumps
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why clusters of cases appear by chance and how investigators check whether one is real.

levels.title: True for the Group, Not for You
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a pattern across groups or places may not hold for the individuals in them.

levels.title: Nobody Is Average
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why almost no one is average on many measures at once, using the US Air Force's 1950 cockpit study.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Statistical Traps
levels.objective: After this level you can explain which trap, from Simpson's paradox to survivorship bias, is at work in a surprising statistic.

levels.title: What Big Data Can and Can't Do
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why huge amounts of data still mislead when they are biased, using Google Flu Trends.

levels.title: A/B Tests: Experiments on You
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how apps and websites run randomized experiments on their users and what those tests can show.

levels.title: What "70% Chance of Rain" Means
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a forecast's percentage means and how a forecaster is checked for being well calibrated.

levels.title: When the Favorite Loses
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a candidate given a 70% chance should still lose about 3 times in 10, and why that doesn't make the forecast wrong.

levels.title: When Algorithms Get It Wrong
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the trade-off between false alarms and misses in a prediction algorithm, and why bias in its data carries through.

levels.title: Reading a Health Headline
levels.objective: After this level you can check a health headline by asking about absolute risk, the study's design and its size.

levels.title: Two Ways to Count Crime
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why police records and victim surveys give different crime numbers and what each misses.

levels.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Math
levels.objective: After this level you can estimate an unknown number by breaking it into simple guesses you can multiply, and use it to sanity-check a claim.

levels.title: Your Checklist for Any Statistic
levels.objective: After this level you can run any number in the news through a short set of questions: of what, compared to what, from whom, and how sure.

levels.title: Mastery Challenge: Probability & Statistics
levels.objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Probability & Statistics Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
